specStatements.text: A force or a system of forces may cause an object to rotate.
Students should be able to describe examples in which forces cause rotation.
The turning effect of a force is called the moment of the force. The size of the moment is defined by the equation:
moment of a force = force × distance
moment of a force, M, in newton-metres, Nm
distance, d, is the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force, in metres, m.
If an object is balanced, the total clockwise moment about a pivot equals the total anticlockwise moment about that pivot.
Students should be able to calculate the size of a force, or its distance from a pivot, acting on an object that is balanced.
A simple lever and a simple gear system can both be used to transmit the rotational effects of forces.
Students should be able to explain how levers and gears transmit the rotational effects of forces.

concepts.definition: A force, or a system of forces, may cause an object to rotate instead of simply moving along a straight line. Rotation happens when the line of action of the force misses the fixed point about which the object can turn, so that the force acts at some perpendicular distance from that point.

The fixed point about which an object turns. A moment is always stated about a particular pivot: the same force can have a large moment about one pivot and no moment at all about another, because the perpendicular distance differs in each case.

The turning effect of a force is called the moment of the force. It measures how strongly a force tends to turn an object about a pivot, and it depends on both the size of the force and its perpendicular distance from the pivot.

The size of the moment is defined by the equation moment of a force = force × distance, written in symbols as M = F d. The two quantities multiply, so doubling either the force or the distance doubles the moment.

concepts.term: Quantities and units in M = F d
concepts.definition: Moment of a force, M, is in newton-metres, Nm. Force, F, is in newtons, N. Distance, d, is in metres, m. A mass given in kilograms must first be converted to a weight in newtons, and a distance given in centimetres or millimetres must be converted to metres, before the equation is used.

In M = F d the distance d is the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force, in metres. It is not necessarily the length of the object, nor the distance measured along the object to the point where the force is applied; when the force acts at an angle to the object the perpendicular distance is shorter than that.

concepts.term: Line of action of a force
concepts.definition: The straight line drawn through the point at which a force acts, along the direction of the force and extended in both directions. The distance d is measured from the pivot at right angles to this line. If the line of action passes through the pivot, d is zero and the moment is zero.

Every force acting on an object turns it about the pivot in one of two senses. A moment that would turn the object clockwise is called a clockwise moment; one that would turn it the other way is an anticlockwise moment. Moments acting in the same sense are added together.

If an object is balanced, the total clockwise moment about a pivot equals the total anticlockwise moment about that pivot. It is the moments that must match, not the forces and not the distances, so a small force far from the pivot can balance a large force close to it.

concepts.term: Finding an unknown force or distance
concepts.definition: For a balanced object, writing total clockwise moment = total anticlockwise moment gives one equation that can be solved for a single unknown. To find a force, divide the known moment by that force's distance; to find a distance, divide the known moment by that force.

A rigid bar that turns about a pivot. A force applied at a large distance from the pivot produces a large moment, which is transmitted through the bar and can move a much larger load acting close to the pivot. The lever transmits the rotational effect of the force; it does not create energy.

Two or more toothed wheels meshed together. The teeth of one wheel push on the teeth of the next, transmitting the rotational effect from one wheel to the other. Meshed gears turn in opposite senses, and a larger driven gear turns more slowly than the smaller driving gear but with a larger moment.

concepts.term: Everyday examples of forces causing rotation
concepts.definition: Pushing the edge of a door so that it swings on its hinges, pressing a bicycle pedal so that the crank turns about the axle, and pulling on a spanner so that a nut turns are all cases in which a force applied at a distance from a pivot causes rotation.

misconceptions.question: A single push is applied to the edge of a gate, well away from its hinges. Can one force on its own make the gate rotate?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. A single force whose line of action does not pass through the pivot has a moment about that pivot, so it can make the object rotate.
misconceptions.misconception: One force on its own can only push something along in a straight line; to make something turn you need two forces, one at each side, like both hands on a steering wheel.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The clearest turning actions students meet are two-handed ones - steering wheels, taps, screw tops - so they generalise that turning needs a pair of forces, and earlier work on resultant forces has trained them to link a single force with straight-line motion.
misconceptions.correction: The specification states that a force or a system of forces may cause an object to rotate. One force is enough, provided its line of action is some perpendicular distance from the pivot: a single push on the edge of a gate swings it about its hinges.

misconceptions.question: A force is applied to a bar at an angle, at a point 0.40 m along the bar from the pivot. Which distance goes into M = F d?
misconceptions.correct: The perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force, which is less than 0.40 m when the force is at an angle.
misconceptions.misconception: The distance is just how far along the object the force is applied, so 0.40 m is what goes into the equation whatever direction the force points in.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Diagrams in textbooks usually show the force at right angles to the bar, where the two distances happen to be equal, so students never have to separate them and read d as 'distance along the bar'.
misconceptions.correction: The specification defines d as the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force. Extend the line of action, then measure from the pivot at right angles to it; only when the force is perpendicular to the bar does this equal the distance along the bar.

misconceptions.question: A large force is applied to a door along a line of action passing straight through the hinge. What is its moment about the hinge?
misconceptions.correct: Zero. The perpendicular distance is zero, so M = F d gives zero however large the force is.
misconceptions.misconception: A force that big must still turn it a bit - a big force always has a big turning effect somewhere.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students treat 'force' and 'turning effect' as the same idea, so a large number for F feels as though it must produce a large turning effect regardless of where the force acts.
misconceptions.correction: The moment depends on the product F d. If the line of action passes through the pivot then d = 0 and the moment is zero, which is why pushing a door close to its hinge is so ineffective.

misconceptions.question: A force of 25 N acts at a perpendicular distance of 15 cm from a pivot. What is the moment about the pivot?
misconceptions.correct: 3.75 Nm. The distance must be converted to metres first: 15 cm = 0.15 m, so M = 25 x 0.15 = 3.75 Nm.
misconceptions.misconception: The numbers can be used exactly as they are printed, so 25 x 15 = 375 and the moment is 375 Nm.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In many earlier calculations the units given already matched the equation, so students are not in the habit of checking, and 'centimetres' and 'metres' both look like ordinary length units on the page.
misconceptions.correction: The specification states that d is in metres and M is in newton-metres. Convert every distance to metres before substituting: 15 cm = 0.15 m gives 3.75 Nm, a hundred times smaller than the unconverted answer.

misconceptions.question: Two children balance on a see-saw. What must be true about their weights and their distances from the pivot?
misconceptions.correct: Their moments must be equal: weight x distance on one side equals weight x distance on the other. The weights themselves need not be equal, nor the distances.
misconceptions.misconception: If it is balanced then the two children must weigh the same, or must be sitting the same distance out from the pivot.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Playground see-saws are usually used by children of similar size sitting at the ends, so the balanced cases students actually see are the symmetrical ones, and 'balanced' gets read as 'the same on both sides'.
misconceptions.correction: The condition is on the moments, not on the forces or the distances separately. A light child far from the pivot balances a heavy child close to it, because the two products weight x distance are equal.

misconceptions.question: A balanced beam carries a large force on one side and a small force on the other. Which force is further from the pivot?
misconceptions.correct: The small force. Its distance must be greater so that its moment matches the moment of the large force acting closer in.
misconceptions.misconception: The bigger force always has the bigger turning effect, so the bigger force must be the one sitting further out.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students reason from the force alone rather than from the product F d, so 'bigger force' is taken to imply 'bigger everything', including distance.
misconceptions.correction: Since the moments are equal and moment = force x distance, the larger force must act at the smaller distance. That is exactly how a crowbar works: a small effort far out balances a large load close in.

misconceptions.question: A 2.0 kg bag hangs 0.30 m from a pivot, where the gravitational field strength is 9.8 N/kg. What is the moment of its weight?
misconceptions.correct: About 5.9 Nm. The weight is 2.0 x 9.8 = 19.6 N, so M = 19.6 x 0.30 = 5.88 Nm.
misconceptions.misconception: The mass is the thing pulling down, so put 2.0 straight into the equation: 2.0 x 0.30 gives a moment of 0.60 Nm.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Mass and weight are used interchangeably in everyday speech, and the kilogram figure is the number printed in the question, so it is the one students reach for.
misconceptions.correction: The specification gives F in newtons. A mass in kilograms must be converted to a weight in newtons using weight = mass x gravitational field strength before it is substituted into M = F d.

misconceptions.question: What is the unit of the moment of a force?
misconceptions.correct: The newton-metre, Nm, as given in the specification.
misconceptions.misconception: A moment is a kind of force, so it must be measured in newtons - or in newtons per metre, since it involves a force and a distance.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'force' appears inside the phrase 'moment of a force', and students meet 'per' units such as N/kg and m/s so often that any two-quantity unit is assumed to be a division.
misconceptions.correction: The moment is a force multiplied by a distance, so its unit is a newton multiplied by a metre: the newton-metre, Nm. It is a turning effect, not a force, and is never measured in newtons.

misconceptions.question: Why is a nut easier to loosen with a long spanner than with a short one?
misconceptions.correct: The same push acts at a greater perpendicular distance from the pivot, so it produces a larger moment.
misconceptions.misconception: The long spanner makes the push itself stronger - the extra length adds force to your hand.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The effect felt by the user is 'it feels easier', which students explain by saying the tool gives them more force, since force is the only quantity they have language for.
misconceptions.correction: The force you apply is unchanged; it is the distance d that increases, and M = F d then gives a larger moment. Levers transmit and increase the turning effect, not the force you exert.

misconceptions.question: A crowbar lets a small push lift a very heavy stone. Where does the extra effect come from?
misconceptions.correct: From the difference in distances. The effort acts far from the pivot and the load close to it, so a small force produces a moment large enough to match the load's moment.
misconceptions.misconception: The lever creates a bigger moment than the one you put in - that is how machines give you something for nothing.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The visible outcome, a small person shifting a heavy load, looks like a gain, and students have no accounting rule that stops them treating machines as sources of extra effect.
misconceptions.correction: The lever transmits the rotational effect of the force; it does not create it. The moment of the effort about the pivot is what moves the load, and the effort must move through a much greater distance than the load does.

misconceptions.question: A small gear wheel drives a larger gear wheel meshed with it. How does the larger gear turn?
misconceptions.correct: More slowly than the small gear, and with a larger moment, because it has more teeth to move round for each turn of the small one.
misconceptions.misconception: The bigger gear turns faster because it is bigger, or both gears turn at the same rate because they are joined together.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students see the rim of the large wheel sweeping a long way and read that as 'faster', and 'joined together' suggests the two wheels must do the same thing.
misconceptions.correction: The teeth mesh, so both gears pass the same number of teeth per second. The larger wheel therefore completes fewer turns per second, and it turns with a larger moment than the smaller driving gear.

misconceptions.question: A moment of 5.0 is calculated from a 25 N force at 0.20 m. Can the answer be given in joules?
misconceptions.correct: No. The moment of a force is given in newton-metres, Nm. Joules are the unit of energy and work done.
misconceptions.misconception: Work done is force x distance and a moment is force x distance, so they are the same thing and either unit will do.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two equations look identical on the page, and students match equations by their shape rather than by what the distances in them mean.
misconceptions.correction: In work done, the distance is measured along the direction of the force; in a moment, it is the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action. They are different quantities, so the moment is given in Nm, not J.

misconceptions.question: A plank balances on a pivot with several weights on it. What has to be added up on each side?
misconceptions.correct: The moments. Each force is multiplied by its own perpendicular distance from the pivot, and the totals on the two sides are then compared.
misconceptions.misconception: Just add up the forces on each side and make those totals match, or compare the biggest weight on each side.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Adding forces is what students practise for months in work on resultant forces, so a balance problem triggers the familiar routine before the new one.
misconceptions.correction: Balance is a condition on moments, not on forces. Each force must first be multiplied by its own distance from the pivot; only then are the clockwise and anticlockwise totals compared.

misconceptions.question: Two gear wheels are meshed together and the first is turned clockwise. Which way does the second turn?
misconceptions.correct: Anticlockwise. Where the teeth meet, the first gear pushes the second the opposite way round.
misconceptions.misconception: They both turn the same way, because the turning effect is simply passed along from one wheel to the next.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students picture the rotation being handed on unchanged, as it is by a belt or a chain, and do not look at the direction in which the teeth actually push at the point of contact.
misconceptions.correction: At the point where the teeth mesh, the surfaces of the two wheels move together, which sends the second wheel round the opposite way. A chain or belt drive keeps the sense the same; meshed teeth reverse it.

misconceptions.question: A metre rule is balanced with the pivot at the 30 cm mark. Is this possible?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Moments can be taken about any pivot, and a balanced object need not be symmetrical about it.
misconceptions.misconception: A balanced object has to be symmetrical - the pivot in the middle and each force the same distance out.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Almost every first example of balance is a symmetrical see-saw, so symmetry becomes part of what students think 'balanced' means.
misconceptions.correction: The condition is that the total clockwise moment about the pivot equals the total anticlockwise moment about that pivot. Any arrangement satisfying that is balanced, symmetrical or not.

misconceptions.question: A moment of 3.0 Nm must be balanced by an 8.0 N force. How far from the pivot does that force act?
misconceptions.correct: 0.375 m. Divide the moment by the force: d = M / F = 3.0 / 8.0.
misconceptions.misconception: Divide the force by the moment instead, or multiply them, since the equation has all three quantities in it anyway.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Rearranging M = F d is done by pattern-matching rather than by algebra, so students pick whichever of the three operations produces a comfortable-looking number.
misconceptions.correction: Rearranging M = F d properly gives d = M / F and F = M / d. Checking the units helps: newton-metres divided by newtons leaves metres, which is what a distance should be.

mcqs.stem: A single steady force is applied to a gate that can swing freely on its hinges. In which case does the gate rotate?

options.text: When the line of action of the force does not pass through the hinges
options.rationale: A force acting at some perpendicular distance from the pivot has a moment about it, so it turns the gate.

options.text: Only when a second force acts on the gate at the same moment
options.rationale: One force is enough: the specification says a force or a system of forces may cause rotation.

options.text: Whenever the force is larger than the weight of the gate itself
options.rationale: Size of force alone decides nothing; a huge force through the hinge still gives no turning effect.

options.text: Only when the force is applied exactly at the middle of the gate
options.rationale: The middle is not special. What matters is the perpendicular distance from the hinges, not the point chosen.

mcqs.stem: Which of these is an example of a force causing an object to rotate?

options.text: A crate being pulled along a level floor by a rope tied to it
options.rationale: The pull is along the line of travel through the crate, so it drags the crate rather than turning it.

options.text: Pushing on the edge of a revolving door to make it turn
options.rationale: The push acts at a distance from the central pivot, so it has a moment and the door rotates.

options.text: Two people pushing a stalled car forwards along a flat road
options.rationale: Both pushes act along the direction of travel, so the car moves in a straight line rather than rotating.

options.text: A ball falling straight downwards after being dropped
options.rationale: The weight acts through the ball's centre, so there is no perpendicular distance and no turning effect.

mcqs.stem: A force acts on a bar that can turn about a pivot. What is the turning effect of that force called?

options.text: The rotational force of the bar at the pivot
options.rationale: There is no such quantity as a rotational force; the turning effect is a moment, measured in Nm.

options.text: The leverage of the force acting on the bar
options.rationale: Leverage is an everyday word, not the term the specification uses for the turning effect.

options.text: The moment of the force about the pivot
options.rationale: The specification states that the turning effect of a force is called the moment of the force.

options.text: The work done by the force on the bar
options.rationale: Work done is an energy transfer in joules, not the turning effect of the force.

mcqs.stem: The size of the moment of a force is defined by which equation?

options.text: moment of a force = weight × distance
options.rationale: The quantity in the equation is the force F in newtons; a weight is only one kind of force.

options.text: moment of a force = force × length of bar
options.rationale: The distance is the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action, not the length of the bar.

options.text: moment of a force = force divided by distance
options.rationale: Dividing would give a unit of newtons per metre; the moment is a force multiplied by a distance, in Nm.

options.text: moment of a force = force × distance
options.rationale: This is the equation exactly as the specification gives it, written in symbols as M = F d.

mcqs.stem: Which row gives the units to use in the equation M = F d?

options.text: M in newton-metres, F in grams, d in metres
options.rationale: The grams figure is a mass; it must be converted to a weight in newtons before it is used as F.

options.text: M in newton-metres, F in newtons, d in metres
options.rationale: These are the units the specification gives: Nm for the moment, N for the force and m for the distance.

options.text: M in newtons, F in newtons, d in metres
options.rationale: The moment is not a force, so it is not in newtons; the specification gives it in newton-metres.

options.text: M in joules, F in newtons, d in metres
options.rationale: Joules are for work done and energy; a moment is stated in newton-metres.

mcqs.stem: A 2.0 kg bag hangs from a beam at a perpendicular distance of 0.30 m from the pivot. The gravitational field strength is 9.8 N/kg. What is the moment of the bag's weight about the pivot?

options.rationale: The mass in kilograms has been substituted for F; 2.0 x 0.30 uses a mass where a force in newtons is required.
The arithmetic is right but the unit is not: a moment is given in newton-metres, not in joules.

options.text: 5.9 Nm
options.rationale: Weight = 2.0 x 9.8 = 19.6 N, so M = F d = 19.6 x 0.30 = 5.88 Nm, which is 5.9 Nm to two significant figures.
This is the weight of the bag, rounded, given as if it were the moment; the moment is not a force in newtons.

mcqs.stem: In the equation M = F d, what exactly is the distance d?

options.text: The distance measured along the object from the pivot to where it acts
options.rationale: That only matches d when the force is at right angles to the object; at an angle it is too large.

options.text: The distance the object moves in the direction of the force as it turns
options.rationale: That is the distance used in work done, not the distance in the moment equation.

options.text: The distance from one end of the object across to its far end
options.rationale: The length of the object is irrelevant; d is measured from the pivot, wherever the pivot happens to be.

options.text: The perpendicular distance from the pivot to its line of action
options.rationale: This is the definition the specification gives, and it is measured in metres.

mcqs.stem: A 60 N push is applied to a door along a line of action that passes exactly through the hinge. Why does the door not turn?

options.text: The perpendicular distance from the hinge is zero
options.rationale: With d = 0, M = F d gives a moment of zero however large the force is.

options.text: The push is too small to overcome the weight of the door
options.rationale: The size of the force is not the problem; the same 60 N applied at the edge would swing the door easily.

options.text: A single force can never make a heavy object rotate
options.rationale: One force is enough to cause rotation, provided its line of action misses the pivot.

options.text: The push is applied too high up on the face of the door
options.rationale: Height above the floor does not matter; what matters is the perpendicular distance from the hinge.

mcqs.stem: A force of 25 N acts at a perpendicular distance of 15 cm from a pivot. What is the moment of the force about the pivot?

options.rationale: The distance has been converted twice, or read as millimetres, giving an answer ten times too small.

options.text: 375 Nm
options.rationale: The centimetres have been used unconverted; 25 x 15 is a hundred times the correct moment.
15 cm = 0.15 m, so M = F d = 25 x 0.15 = 3.75 Nm, with the distance in metres as the specification requires.
This is just the force copied out, in newtons; the moment is a force multiplied by a distance, in Nm.

mcqs.stem: A gardener prises up a stone using a long-handled spade as a lever. Why is a long handle better than a short one?

options.text: The longer handle increases the size of the push the gardener makes
options.rationale: The push is set by the gardener and is unchanged; it is the distance from the pivot that has increased.

options.text: The lever gives out more energy than the gardener puts into it
options.rationale: No machine does that. The lever transmits the rotational effect; the effort simply moves much further.

options.text: A longer handle is heavier, so it presses on the stone harder
options.rationale: The handle's own weight is not what lifts the stone; the moment of the gardener's push does.

options.text: The same push acts at a greater distance, so its moment is larger
options.rationale: M = F d, so increasing d while F stays the same increases the turning effect on the stone.

mcqs.stem: An object is balanced about a pivot. Which statement must be true?

options.text: The total clockwise moment equals the total anticlockwise moment
options.rationale: This is the balanced condition exactly as the specification states it, about that same pivot.

options.text: The total of the forces on one side equals the total on the other side
options.rationale: Forces are added in resultant force problems; balance about a pivot is a condition on moments.

options.text: Each force must act the same distance from the pivot as the other one
options.rationale: Equal distances are only needed when the forces are equal; unequal forces balance at unequal distances.

options.text: The pivot must be exactly at the middle of the whole object
options.rationale: A balanced object need not be symmetrical; moments can be taken about any pivot.

mcqs.stem: A plank balances on a pivot. A 10 N weight sits 0.60 m to the left of the pivot, and a 30 N weight sits somewhere to the right. What can be said about the 30 N weight?

options.text: It sits further from the pivot, because a larger force turns more
options.rationale: The larger force already supplies a larger moment per metre, so it must act closer in, not further out.

options.text: It sits closer to the pivot, because its force is the larger
options.rationale: Equal moments with a larger force means a smaller distance: 0.20 m, one third of 0.60 m.

options.text: It sits the same distance out, as the plank is balanced
options.rationale: Equal distances would give unequal moments here, and the plank would tip to the right.

options.text: It cannot balance, since the two forces are not equal
options.rationale: Balance needs equal moments, not equal forces; unequal forces balance at suitable distances.

mcqs.stem: A beam is balanced on a pivot. A 100 N weight hangs 0.75 m to the left of the pivot, and a single weight hangs 1.5 m to the right. What is that weight?

options.rationale: The two forces have been set equal to each other; it is the moments that must be equal, not the forces.
The rearrangement has been done the wrong way round, dividing the distance by the moment.
All three numbers have been multiplied together, 100 x 0.75 x 1.5, instead of dividing the moment by the distance.
Anticlockwise moment = 100 x 0.75 = 75 Nm, so the unknown weight is 75 / 1.5 = 50 N.

mcqs.stem: A rod is balanced on a pivot. A 6.0 N force acts 0.50 m from the pivot on one side, and an 8.0 N force acts on the other side. How far from the pivot is the 8.0 N force?

options.rationale: Clockwise moment = 6.0 x 0.50 = 3.0 Nm, so d = M / F = 3.0 / 8.0 = 0.375 m.
The 8.0 N and 6.0 N have been swapped in the rearrangement, giving 8.0 x 0.50 / 6.0.
The two distances have been set equal; equal distances with unequal forces would not balance.
The moment has been multiplied by the force instead of divided by it, 3.0 x 8.0.

mcqs.stem: What do a simple lever and a simple gear system have in common?

options.text: Both give out more energy than is put into them by the user
options.rationale: Neither creates energy; each transmits a turning effect, with the effort moving a greater distance.

options.text: Both can be used to transmit the rotational effects of forces
options.rationale: This is what the specification says about them: each transmits the turning effect from one place to another.

options.text: Both increase the size of the force that you apply to them
options.rationale: The applied force is unchanged. What is changed is the moment, through the distance from the pivot.

options.text: Both change a force's direction without turning anything
options.rationale: Turning is exactly what they do; that is why moments are needed to describe them.

mcqs.stem: Two gear wheels are meshed together and the smaller one is driven clockwise. How does the larger gear turn?

options.text: Clockwise too, because the teeth push it the same way round
options.rationale: At the point where the teeth mesh the push is the other way, so the second wheel turns the opposite way.

options.text: Anticlockwise but faster, because it is the bigger wheel
options.rationale: Both wheels pass the same number of teeth each second, so the larger wheel turns more slowly.

options.text: Anticlockwise, more slowly, and with a larger moment
options.rationale: Meshed teeth reverse the sense; the larger wheel makes fewer turns per second and exerts a larger moment.

options.text: Anticlockwise and slower, so its moment is smaller too
options.rationale: Turning more slowly does not mean a smaller moment; the larger gear turns with a larger moment.
